stem_html:
The committee's report is ______ in its criticism: it names no official, assigns no date to any failure, and recommends that procedures be reviewed. Every sentence in it could have been written before the disaster it investigates.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "unspecific"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "scathing", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "reluctant", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "measured", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Three absences, one property. The list after the colon is the definition of the blank.
  • A word about tone where the sentence is about content.
  • The final sentence is the strongest evidence and it comes after the blank.

Why A is right The colon lists three absences — no official, no date, no concrete recommendation — and the last sentence generalises: every sentence in it could have been written before the disaster it investigates. That is criticism without particulars.

Why B is wrong Scathing describes criticism that lands hard. The evidence describes criticism that never touches anything, which is the opposite property.

Why C is wrong Reluctant attributes an attitude to the committee. The sentence describes the report's content rather than the writers' willingness, and a reluctant report could still name names.

Why D is wrong Measured is a compliment for restraint. The passage is not praising proportion; it is pointing out that nothing in the report is attached to the events.

stem_html:
Fossil trackways ______ what skeletons cannot: a skeleton gives the shape of a foot, but only a trackway records how fast the animal was moving and whether it walked alone.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "preserve"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "obscure", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "resemble", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "predict", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “What skeletons cannot” is elliptical. The verb in the blank has to be the one the ellipsis repeats.
  • The colon defines the blank, and the definition is about recording.
  • A negative reading of a positive sentence.

Why A is right The clause after the colon says only a trackway records how fast the animal was moving, so the trackways hold information the bones do not. Preserve is what a record does.

Why B is wrong Obscure would mean the trackways hide something. The sentence credits them with keeping information available.

Why C is wrong Resemble compares the two kinds of fossil, and the sentence contrasts what each one contains. Similarity of appearance is not at issue.

Why D is wrong Predict points forward in time. A trackway records behaviour that already happened; nothing here is being forecast.

stem_html:
Bernal's translation is ______ where the original is plain. The Nahuatl poem uses one verb four times in eight lines; Bernal supplies four different English verbs, each more ornate than the last, and the repetition that gave the poem its insistence disappears.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "elaborate"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "literal", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "inaccurate", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "concise", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Where the original is plain” is a contrast, and two choices restate plainness.
  • A stronger charge than the evidence carries. Ornament is not error.
  • The lost repetition is what the last clause is grieving, and it points at variety rather than at inaccuracy.

Why A is right The blank is set against “plain,” and the evidence is four different English verbs, each more ornate than the last. Elaborate is the quality that opposes plainness.

Why B is wrong Literal would make the translation closer to the original, and the sentence says it differs from it. A literal version would have repeated the one verb.

Why C is wrong Inaccurate is a judgement the passage almost supports and does not make. The four verbs may all be defensible renderings; the complaint is about ornament and lost repetition.

Why D is wrong Concise is a second synonym for plain, so it would make the sentence say the translation is plain where the original is plain, which contradicts “where.”

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 article about urban heat.

Planting street trees is the standard municipal response to summer heat, and the standard measure of success is canopy cover. Ferrante's instrumented survey of eleven Madrid streets found that canopy cover predicted daytime shade well and predicted night-time temperature not at all: the streets that stayed coolest after dark were the ones with the least paved surface, whatever their canopy. Since heat deaths cluster at night, Ferrante argues that a canopy target measures the half of the problem that kills fewer people.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It reports a finding that a standard success measure misses the part of the problem that matters most."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It argues that cities should stop planting street trees.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It explains how canopy cover is measured in urban heat surveys.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It compares daytime and night-time temperatures in eleven Madrid streets.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Criticising a measure is not criticising the thing measured.
  • The finding is mixed. Canopy predicts one thing well and another not at all, and only one choice keeps both halves.
  • Evidence promoted to purpose.

Why A is right The passage names the measure, shows what it fails to predict, and draws the consequence: a canopy target measures the half of the problem that kills fewer people.

Why B is wrong Ferrante criticises the target, not the trees. The finding is that canopy predicts daytime shade well, which is a benefit, and nothing recommends stopping.

Why C is wrong No method of measurement is described. Canopy cover is named as the criterion and its predictive value is what the passage examines.

Why D is wrong The day-night comparison is the evidence, and eleven streets is the sample. Neither is the point, which is what the comparison shows about the target.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from Kate Chopin's 1899 novel The Awakening.

In short, Mrs. Pontellier was beginning to realize her position in the universe as a human being, and to recognize her relations as an individual to the world within and about her. This may seem like a ponderous weight of wisdom to descend upon the soul of a young woman of twenty-eight — perhaps more wisdom than the Holy Ghost is usually pleased to vouchsafe to any woman.

Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It anticipates a reader's objection to the first sentence and answers it with irony directed at the objection."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It concedes that the first sentence overstates the character's self-awareness.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It explains why the character has taken until the age of twenty-eight to reach this understanding.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It introduces a religious framework that governs the rest of the passage.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Irony read as agreement. The sentence sounds like a concession and is not one.
  • “May seem” is the marker of a voiced objection, not of the narrator's own view.
  • A single ironic reference is not a framework.

Why A is right “This may seem like a ponderous weight of wisdom” voices the reader's likely doubt, and the clause about what the Holy Ghost is usually pleased to vouchsafe to any woman mocks the assumption behind it rather than conceding to it.

Why B is wrong The sentence does not concede. Its irony puts the burden on whoever finds the claim implausible, which is the opposite of retracting it.

Why C is wrong No cause for the timing is given. Twenty-eight is named to make the objection vivid, not to explain a delay.

Why D is wrong The Holy Ghost appears once, inside the ironic clause. Nothing in the passage builds a framework from it.

Text 1

The written record of the Bronze Age collapse names invaders, and archaeology finds burned citadels in the same decades. The simplest reading is the oldest one: a wave of raiders brought the palace economies down.

Text 2

Aguilar does not dispute the burning. She points out that a palace economy holds no more than a season's grain, and that three independent climate records show consecutive failed harvests across the eastern Mediterranean in exactly those decades. A population that has already stopped receiving rations, she argues, burns its own citadel.

Based on the texts, how would Aguilar (Text 2) most likely respond to the reading offered in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By arguing that the physical evidence it relies on is equally consistent with an internal cause."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "By denying that the citadels were burned in the decades the written record names.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "By agreeing that raiders were responsible but adding that drought made them more effective.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By showing that the written record was composed long after the events it describes.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Same evidence, different cause is the shape of the disagreement.
  • Adding a factor instead of replacing one.
  • An attack on the sources that Text 2 never makes.

Why A is right Aguilar accepts the burning and supplies a different agent for it: a population that has already stopped receiving rations burns its own citadel. Same evidence, second explanation.

Why B is wrong She opens by not disputing the burning, so denying it would throw away the fact she is reinterpreting.

Why C is wrong This keeps the raiders as the cause and demotes the harvest failures to a contributing factor. Her argument replaces the agent rather than assisting it.

Why D is wrong The date of composition is never raised in Text 2. Her case is built from grain storage and climate records.

stem_html:
Neuroscientist Petra Lindqvist proposed that songbirds sleep less during migration without accumulating a sleep debt because they take hundreds of very short naps in flight, and that these naps do the restorative work that longer sleep does at rest.

Which finding, if true, would most directly support Lindqvist's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Birds whose in-flight recordings showed the most microsleep episodes performed as well on post-migration learning tasks as birds that had not migrated, while migrating birds with the fewest episodes performed worse."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Migrating birds slept far fewer total hours than non-migrating birds of the same species.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Migrating birds showed hundreds of brief episodes of one-hemisphere sleep during flight.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Non-migrating birds deprived of sleep for one night performed worse on learning tasks the following day.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Existence against function. Showing the naps occur is not showing they do the work.
  • Restating the phenomenon. Less total sleep is the thing being explained.
  • A control condition offered as evidence for a claim about a different population.

Why A is right Lindqvist proposed that these naps do the restorative work that longer sleep does at rest, so the proposal claims the naps do restorative work, so the evidence has to link the number of naps to a restoration outcome. More episodes with intact performance and fewer episodes with impaired performance is exactly that link.

Why B is wrong Reduced total sleep is the puzzle, not the answer. It is agreed by everyone and says nothing about what makes the reduction survivable.

Why C is wrong This establishes that the naps happen, which is half the proposal. It leaves open whether they restore anything.

Why D is wrong This is about non-migrating birds and ordinary sleep deprivation. It supports the general importance of sleep without bearing on whether microsleeps substitute for it.

stem_html:
An economist argues that a city's 2019 rent cap did not reduce the number of rental units, contrary to predictions, because landlords who would have converted flats to short-term lets were already prevented from doing so by a separate 2017 ordinance.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the economist's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "In comparable cities with a rent cap but no short-term-let ordinance, the number of rental units fell after the cap was imposed."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The number of rental units in the city was unchanged in the three years after 2019.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Rents in the city rose more slowly after 2019 than in comparable cities without a cap.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The 2017 ordinance was opposed by landlord associations at the time it was passed.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The explanation names a second policy, so the evidence has to vary that policy.
  • Confirming the outcome instead of the mechanism.
  • A different outcome variable. Rents are not units.

Why A is right The economist argues that landlords who would have converted flats to short-term lets were already prevented from doing so by a separate 2017 ordinance, so the ordinance is what protected the stock, so the test is what happens where the ordinance is absent. Units falling in cities with a cap and no ordinance is the comparison the claim needs.

Why B is wrong Unchanged stock is the fact being explained. It is common ground and cannot distinguish the economist's explanation from any other.

Why C is wrong Rent levels are a different outcome. The argument is about the number of units, and a cap can hold rents down whatever happens to supply.

Why D is wrong Opposition to the ordinance says nothing about its effect. Landlords oppose measures that work and measures that do not.

stem_html:
Researchers measured how many words per minute readers could process from four presentation formats. They concluded that reading speed depends on line length rather than on font size.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the researchers' conclusion?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Both short-line formats were read about 55 words per minute faster than both long-line formats, while the two font sizes differed by no more than 4 words per minute within each line length."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The short line at 11 point was read faster than the long line at 14 point.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The 14-point formats were read faster than the 11-point formats.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Every format was read at more than 200 words per minute.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two factors, and the comparison has to hold one fixed.
  • The font-size differences run in opposite directions at the two line lengths, which is what “no effect” looks like.
  • A true reading that tests nothing.

Why A is right They concluded that reading speed depends on line length rather than on font size, which has a positive half and a negative half, and this choice supplies both: a large and consistent gap by line length, and a difference of at most 4 words per minute by font size.

Why B is wrong This single comparison varies both factors at once, so it cannot show which of them is responsible.

Why C is wrong It is not even true of the whole graph — the 14-point short line was slower than the 11-point short line — and it asserts the effect the conclusion denies.

Why D is wrong A floor that every format clears says nothing about either variable.

stem_html: In his novel The Quarry, Ansel Bright characterizes the foreman as someone whose authority rests on withholding information rather than on any formal rank. Which quotation from a fictional novel would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“He alone knew which face they would open next, and he let the question stand until the men had guessed wrong twice.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“He had been foreman for eleven years, and the company had never once put his name on a document.”", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“He gave the order and the men obeyed it, as they had obeyed his father before him.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“He kept the ledgers locked, though anyone who asked could have the key for the asking.”", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The claim has a positive and a negative half, and the negative half alone is easy to illustrate.
  • A gesture of secrecy that is not one. The concession in D undoes it.
  • Inherited obedience is the alternative source of authority the claim denies.

Why A is right Bright characterizes the foreman as someone whose authority rests on withholding information rather than on any formal rank, and knowing what others do not is authority built out of withholding: he let the question stand until the men had guessed wrong twice. Nothing about rank enters.

Why B is wrong The absence of formal rank is half the claim and the more quotable half. The quotation supplies no withheld information and no authority exercised.

Why C is wrong Obedience inherited from a father is authority from position and custom, which is the kind the claim rules out.

Why D is wrong Locked ledgers look like withholding until the second clause removes it: anyone who asked could have the key. Nothing is actually being kept back.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2022 article about medieval account books.

The household rolls of great English estates were long read as budget documents, and historians have used their totals to estimate what a lord's household consumed. Working through the rolls of four estates, Sandoval finds that the totals were copied forward from year to year: the fish entry for 1319 is the fish entry for 1314, to the penny, in a year when the fishponds were drained. The rolls, she concludes, record what the household was entitled to draw rather than what it drew, which makes them a poor source for consumption and an excellent one for expectation.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Household rolls record entitlements rather than actual consumption, so they answer a different question from the one historians have asked of them."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Historians have miscalculated the totals in medieval household rolls.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The fishponds on one estate were drained in 1319.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Medieval household rolls are unreliable and should not be used as historical sources.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Poor source for X and excellent one for Y” is a reclassification, not a dismissal.
  • The vivid detail is evidence. The fishponds prove the entry was copied.
  • An error of arithmetic against an error of interpretation.

Why A is right The last sentence states it: the rolls record what the household was entitled to draw rather than what it drew, which makes them a poor source for consumption and an excellent one for expectation.

Why B is wrong Nobody's arithmetic is questioned. The totals are accurate copies; the problem is what they are totals of.

Why C is wrong The drained fishponds are the detail that proves the copying, offered inside the sentence that makes the argument.

Why D is wrong Sandoval calls them an excellent source for expectation, which is the opposite of discarding them.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2019 article about the painter Hilma af Klint.

Af Klint's abstract canvases predate Kandinsky's by four years, and the usual explanation for her absence from histories of abstraction is her will, which forbade exhibition for twenty years after her death. Malmberg's work in the foundation's papers complicates that account. Af Klint showed the paintings privately throughout the 1920s, to audiences that included two museum directors, and the letters record their refusals. The will delayed publication; the gatekeepers had already declined.

According to the text, what does Malmberg's research indicate about af Klint's absence from histories of abstraction?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "It began before her will took effect, because people in a position to exhibit the work had already turned it down."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "It was caused entirely by the twenty-year restriction in her will.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "It resulted from her decision not to show the paintings to anyone during her lifetime.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "It has been corrected by recent exhibitions of her work.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The standard account is stated first and qualified second.
  • “Complicates” is not “refutes.” The will still delayed publication.
  • Private showing is still showing, and one choice denies it happened.

Why A is right The last sentence puts the two causes in order: the will delayed publication, and the gatekeepers had already declined. Malmberg's letters show refusals during the 1920s, before the will could operate.

Why B is wrong This is the usual explanation the passage introduces in order to complicate. Malmberg does not deny the will mattered; she shows it was not first.

Why C is wrong She showed the paintings privately throughout the 1920s, so the claim that she showed them to nobody is contradicted by the evidence.

Why D is wrong Recent exhibitions are not mentioned. The passage stops at the letters.

stem_html:
A drug is metabolised by an enzyme that some people produce in unusually large amounts. In a trial, the drug reduced symptoms in 62 percent of participants overall. Among participants who carry the high-activity version of the enzyme, the figure was 24 percent, and among the rest it was 71 percent. The trial enrolled participants without testing for the variant, and the two groups did not differ in age, severity or dose. It follows that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the overall figure understates how well the drug works in people without the high-activity variant."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the drug is ineffective in most people.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "the high-activity variant makes the underlying condition more severe.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the drug should be given at a higher dose to everyone.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A pooled average hides two populations. The overall figure belongs to neither subgroup.
  • The passage rules out the confounds explicitly, which is what makes the inference available.
  • From a finding to a prescription is a step the evidence does not license.

Why A is right The overall 62 percent is a blend of 24 and 71. Since the participants without the variant responded at 71 percent, the pooled figure is dragged down by the carriers and understates the effect in everyone else.

Why B is wrong 62 percent overall and 71 percent in the larger group are both majorities, so “most people” contradicts the numbers given.

Why C is wrong The passage says the two groups did not differ in age, severity or dose. The variant affects the response to the drug, not the condition itself.

Why D is wrong No dose-response information appears, and raising the dose for people who already respond at 71 percent is not supported by anything here.

stem_html:
A library replaced its paper request slips with a terminal. Requests rose by a third in the following month, but the number of volumes actually collected from the desk did not change. Staff report that the terminal allows a reader to submit a request in about four seconds, against roughly a minute for a slip. This suggests that some of the additional requests ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "were made speculatively by readers who would not have judged them worth the effort of a slip."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "were for volumes the library did not hold.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "were made by readers who had never used the library before.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "were duplicates of requests already submitted on paper.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Requests up, collections flat. The gap is the whole finding.
  • The four seconds is the causal detail, and it is about effort rather than about who is asking.
  • A specific mechanism the passage never mentions.

Why A is right The number of volumes actually collected from the desk did not change, and the one thing that changed is the cost of asking, from a minute to four seconds, and collections did not rise. Requests that are made when they are cheap and abandoned at the desk are speculative ones.

Why B is wrong Nothing indicates the requests could not be filled. If they had failed at the catalogue stage they would not have reached the desk to be uncollected.

Why C is wrong New readers would explain more requests and would also be expected to collect some of them. The passage gives no information about who the requesters were.

Why D is wrong Duplicates would be a special case of the answer and the paper slips are gone, so there is nothing to duplicate. The passage offers no evidence of repeated requests.

The instrument measures three things at once ______ wind speed, air temperature, and the concentration of water vapour at the sensor head.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ": wind"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; wind", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": ", wind", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "wind", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A complete clause before the list is what makes the colon legal.
  • A list is not a clause, so the semicolon has nothing to join.
  • Commas already separate the items, so one more at the front is ambiguous.

Why A is right The first clause is complete and announces a list without giving it; a colon after an independent clause is the mark that introduces the list.

Why B is wrong A semicolon joins two independent clauses. What follows is a list of noun phrases, not a clause.

Why C is wrong A comma would make the first list item continuous with the sentence and leave the reader unsure whether “wind speed” is a fourth thing or the first of three.

Why D is wrong With no punctuation the sentence runs “three things at once wind speed,” which cannot be parsed.

stem_html:
Because the samples were stored at room temperature for six weeks before anyone thought to freeze them ______ the results of the assay cannot be compared with those of the earlier study.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", the"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "; the", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": ": the", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "the", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Length is not independence. Six weeks and two verbs do not make the opening a sentence.
  • The subordinator is the first word and decides everything after it.
  • Cause invites a colon, and a colon still needs a full clause in front of it.

Why A is right The opening clause begins with “Because” and is therefore subordinate. An introductory subordinate clause takes a comma before the main clause.

Why B is wrong A semicolon requires an independent clause on its left, and this one cannot stand alone.

Why C is wrong A colon has the same requirement, and the relationship here is cause rather than specification in any case.

Why D is wrong The clause is long enough that omitting the comma runs the subordinate clause into the main one, which Standard English punctuates.

The novel's narrator, an unnamed clerk who never leaves the building ______ the reader nothing about his own past.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

stem_html:
The two techniques give the same answer for shallow water ______ about forty metres the acoustic method drifts and the optical one does not.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "; below"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", below", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "below", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ", but below", "trap": "half-right"}]

  • Both halves stand alone, which is the only test that matters.
  • An adverbial opening on the right of the break makes the second clause look subordinate.

Why C is wrong With no punctuation the reader attaches “below about forty metres” to the first clause and has to reparse.

Why D is wrong “But” with a comma is grammatical, and it is not offered that way here: the choice supplies a comma before “but,” which is correct punctuation, but the sentence then reads as though the contrast were between the two techniques rather than between two depth ranges.

stem_html:
The sequence of tunnels beneath the cathedral, which archaeologists have mapped but not excavated, ______ thought to date from the seventh century.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "is"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "are", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "have been", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "were", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]

Traps in this question

  • The subject is four words from the front and eleven from the verb.

choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Ozawa was known for the attention he paid to the lower strings."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "the lower strings received particular attention from Ozawa.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "it was the lower strings that Ozawa paid the most attention to.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "attention to the lower strings became Ozawa's signature.", "trap": "modifier-attachment"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Ozawa appears in all four. Only one puts him in the subject slot.
  • Passive and cleft constructions are where dangling modifiers hide.
  • An abstract noun as subject reads naturally and cannot be trained.

Why A is right The opening phrase describes a person trained as a cellist, so the subject of the main clause must be Ozawa.

Why B is wrong The subject is “the lower strings,” which cannot have trained as a cellist.

Why C is wrong The subject is the expletive “it,” which has no content for the modifier to describe.

Why D is wrong The subject is “attention,” an abstraction that cannot have turned to conducting.

stem_html:
When the expedition reached the pass in October, the route they had planned to follow ______ under two metres of snow for a fortnight.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "had lain"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "has lain", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "lies", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "will have lain", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “When ... reached” fixes the later event, and the fortnight of snow precedes it.
  • The relative clause is already past perfect, which is a signal rather than a distraction.
  • Three choices place the clause outside the past.

Why A is right The snow covered the route before the expedition arrived, so the earlier of two past events takes the past perfect. “Had planned” earlier in the sentence is already in that tense.

Why B is wrong The present perfect connects to the present, and the sentence is closed in October of a past year.

Why C is wrong Simple present puts a past condition in the reader's own time.

Why D is wrong The future perfect looks back from a point still ahead, which no part of this sentence occupies.

The report compares the two reactors' safety records and concludes that ______ is the better documented of the two, though not necessarily the safer.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "the older reactor's record"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "its record", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "their record", "trap": "pronoun-ambiguity"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "it's record", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two candidates, one pronoun.
  • “Of the two” requires a single referent, which rules out the plural.
  • The apostrophe that is never possessive.

Why A is right Two reactors are being compared, so a pronoun cannot indicate which record is meant. Naming one of them is what makes the sentence informative.

Why B is wrong “Its” could point to either reactor, and the sentence supplies nothing to decide.

Why C is wrong “Their” refers to both reactors, which contradicts “the better documented of the two.”

Why D is wrong “It's” is a contraction of “it is” and cannot show possession.

stem_html:
Deep-sea mining licences are granted on the strength of environmental baseline surveys, and regulators treat a completed survey as evidence that the risks are understood. ______ a review of forty such surveys found that the median one sampled a single season and identified fewer than a tenth of the species later recovered from the same site.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "However,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Consequently,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Similarly,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Indeed,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A reported practice, then evidence against it.
  • “Indeed” is the near-miss: it introduces striking evidence, but evidence that agrees.
  • Consequence where there is contradiction.

Why A is right The review undercuts the regulators' treatment of the surveys, so the transition marks opposition.

Why B is wrong “Consequently” makes the review a result of the regulators' practice, which reverses evidence and cause.

Why C is wrong “Similarly” asserts agreement between the two sentences, and they conflict.

Why D is wrong “Indeed” intensifies the preceding claim. The second sentence weakens it instead.

stem_html:
Glass recycling saves more energy per tonne than almost any other material stream, since remelting cullet needs far less heat than making glass from sand. ______ glass is heavy, and the emissions from trucking it to a distant plant can cancel the saving.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "On the other hand,"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "For instance,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "As a result,", "trap": "transition-reversal"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "In short,", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A benefit, then its offset.
  • An example of the first claim would have to save energy, not spend it.
  • Summary against qualification.

Why A is right The second sentence supplies a countervailing consideration to the first, so the transition has to mark the turn.

Why B is wrong Weight and haulage are not an example of energy saving; they are a reason the saving may not be realised.

Why C is wrong “As a result” would make the emissions a consequence of the energy saving, which they are not.

Why D is wrong “In short” announces a summary, and the second sentence introduces new information that cuts the other way.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Sea otters eat sea urchins.
  • Sea urchins graze on kelp holdfasts.
  • Otters were hunted to near extinction along the North Pacific coast by 1911.
  • Where otters have returned, kelp forest area has increased roughly twentyfold.
  • Kelp forests store carbon and shelter juvenile fish.

The student wants to explain the mechanism by which otters affect kelp. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By preying on the sea urchins that graze kelp holdfasts, otters allow kelp forests to expand; where otters have returned, kelp area has grown roughly twentyfold."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Kelp forests store carbon and shelter juvenile fish, and their area has increased roughly twentyfold where otters have returned.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Sea otters were hunted to near extinction along the North Pacific coast by 1911, and kelp forests declined as a result.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Sea otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins graze on kelp holdfasts.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A mechanism needs every link and the outcome.
  • Consequences of kelp are not part of the chain that produces it.
  • Two premises without the inference is the commonest way to answer a mechanism question wrong.

Why A is right A mechanism is a chain, and this choice states every link: otters eat urchins, urchins eat holdfasts, so removing urchins lets kelp expand — with the twentyfold figure as confirmation.

Why B is wrong Carbon and fish are consequences of kelp forests, not steps in the chain from otters to kelp. The mechanism is missing.

Why C is wrong The hunting is history rather than mechanism, and the causal claim it adds is not in the notes in that form.

Why D is wrong The two links are here and the conclusion is not. The reader is left to work out what follows for the kelp.
